div.p: Bounded response time is an important consideration in applying rule-based expert systems to real-time applications. This paper contributes to response time analysis of expert systems in several ways. The first contribution is the introduction of the rule-based production system MRL. MRL has been designed to facilitate more accurate analysis of the response times of programs while maintaining the flexibility and expressiveness of traditional production systems such as OPS5. The second contribution is research on modular analysis of rule-based systems. Several timing analysis algorithms based on this approach have been developed. One of them, a fixed point detection algorithm is discussed to show that efficient and effective analysis of MRL programs can be achieved. In particular, a general technique called the transfer principle is introduced for exploiting analysis algorithms which are simpler to analyze.
The third contribution is the design of the match algorithm Rhyme. It is a match algorithm uniquely suited for more accurate analysis of the performance of real-time expert systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Although expert systems are increasingly used to monitor real-time applications (e.g., the Air Robotics Vehicle, the Space Shuttle), there has been little work in the formal verification and validation of the performance of expert systems in the real-time environment. In these applications, an expert system monitors the external environment through *This project is supported by research grants from Office of Naval Research under ONR contract numberN00014-89-J-1472as well as ONR contract number N000014-89-J-1913, and also by a grant from Texas Instruments Corporation.

sensors. A change in the environment may trigger a number of rule firings which are required to reconcile the internal state of the expert system to the changed environment. If the number of rule firings is too large or if it takes too much time to select and fire the rules, the environment might have already changed so much that the result of the rule firings would become obsolete. Hence it is important to be able to analyze how fast an expert system can react to a change in the environment.

In more complex decision systems, the usefulness of the result of some iterative computation may depend on the time available for performing the computation e.g., the accuracy of a diagnosis by an expert system may depend on the number of fault hypotheses that get examined. In these cases, it is extremely useful to be able to quantify the performance of an expert system, given a time budget for firing rules. Again, the question boils down to examining how fast an expert system can react to a change. In this paper, we are going to report on an expert system language called MRL that is especially amenable to timing analysis.

div.head: Motivation
div.p: There are two main difficulties for bounding the response times of expert systems (the time required for the working memory to become stable). First, the contents of the working memory of an expert system changes continually and the working memory varies in size with each rule firing. Second, unlike procedural languages, the control flow of expert system programs is embedded in the data and cannot be easily derived. It can also be implementation-dependent. With current expert system languages, it is indeed an uphill battle to perform response time analysis.
We have designed a rule-based production language called MRL (Mucro Rule-based Language) [8] for realtime applications. MRL builds on the language EQL [5].

Whereas the execution model of EQL is a decision table which reads from and writes into a simple dictionary of (variablename, value) pairs, the execution model of MRL resembles more that of OPS5-like languages in that it has pattern variables and its working memory may vary in size and content. However, MRL is different from OPS5like languages in that the semantics of MRL is a simple extension of that of EQL. In particular, for any given working memory, an MRL program can be instantiated into an equivalent EQL program by macro expansion of its rules. This has several important advantages:

The response time of an MRL program can be analyzed by parameterizing the response time of the corresponding EQL programs by the size of the working memory. Since we have a much better handle on EQL owing to its simple execution model, the analysis of MRL is also made manageable.

We can apply known techniques for analyzing EQL programs to the analysis of MRL programs by the following transfer principle. Suppose we know that if an EQL program satisfies a certain property P, then that program must have bounded response time. Suppose further that the MRL program we want to analyze always expands into equivalent EQL programs which satisfy P. Then the semantics of MRL will allow us to conclude immediately that the MRL program will have bounded response time. The corresponding bound often falls out directly from the EQL analysis.

div.head: J.
div.p: A way to control the response time of an expert system is to limit the size of the working memory by setting some criteria for accepting new working memory elements. This can be accomplished by means of a filter which may be dynamically adjusted to keep the size of the working memory manageable, e.g., by throwing out less reliable data from a noisy sensor. This is in keeping with the semantics of MRL since the working set is used simply as an input to macroexpand an MRL program into an EQL program at the beginning of every MRL execution cycle. (An MRL cycle ends when the working memory becomes stable after a number of rule firings.) In this paper, we shall not discuss the issue of how to use the response time analysis to help adjust the working memory input filter, since this can be most effectively done by exploiting the semantics of the application.

A practical difficulty in bounding the response time of expert system programs is the variability of the time to perform the match operation for detecting enabled rules. The EQL-like semantics of MRL should help in this case since the match algorithm can take advantage of the structure of the macro expansion. However, the question remains as to how to design an efficient match algoriEhm for which we can obtain good time bounds. For this purpose, we shall discuss a new match algorithm called Rhyme later in this paper.
Owing to space limitation, we shall omit some details of the language MRL and the proofs of the theorems stated in this paper. Interested readers are referred to the technical reports [7, 10,9].

In section 2, we shall introduce the language EQL which forms the core of the MRL language. Section 3 explains the execution model of the MRL language in terms of the EQL engine. Section 4 introduces the transfer principle. Section 5 discusses a timing analysis algorithm for EQL programs and it will be used in section 6 as an example to demonstrate the tranger principle. Section 7 briefly discusses the match algorithm Rhyme. Section 8 is the conclusion.

div.head: The MRL Model
div.p: The syntax of MRL programs is much the same as that of EQL programs. The most important feature in MRL that distinguishes MRL from EQL is the use of macro variables. Macro variables are similar to the working memory in OPS5. Each macro variable represents a set of primitive variables called expanded variables or working memory elements (wme). Rules that contain macro variables are macro rules (in contrast to plain rules in EQL programs). Conceptually, we model the execution of MRL programs as follows: At the beginning of each cycle, a macro rule is expanded to a set of plain rules each of which contains one of the possible combinations of macro variable expansions (i.e., each macro variable is instantiated to one of the corresponding expanded variables). The result of the expansion is an equivalent EQL program which has the same behavior as the MRL program. Macro variables make it more convenient to assemble related input data into data structures, and also allow us to introducelogical quantifiers, either existential quantifrers or universal quantifrers, a feature absent in EQL. The combination of macro variables and logical quantifiers makes MRL a sufficiently powerful production language for writing OPS5-type real-time expert systems.

We shall introduce the language MRL by an example. Macro variables can be referred to only by special symbols called pattern variables. Pattem variables are, in fact, not real variables because they do not occupy memory space. They are solely used as symbols that refer to macro variables. Two occurrences of the same pattem variable in a rule have to be instantiated to the same expanded variable if they are existentially quantified. The scopes of pattem variables are restricted to one rule only. In the example above, the PATTERN-VAR section declares two pattern variables x and y for the macro variable myiec.
Pattem variables must be quantified when they are used in MRL rules. The pattem variables with a prefix of a question mark, "?", are existentially quantifred variables.

The pattem variables with a prefix of an asterisk, "*", are universally quantified variables. Existentially quantified variables may appear anywhere in a rule. Each existentially quantified pattern variable has to be instantiated to one of the expanded variables of the corresponding macro variable when the rule is fired. On the other hand, universally quantified pattern variables can only appear in the enabling conditions. A rule is enabled if its enabling condition is always true for all possible instantiations of the universally quantified variables.

Let the size of the working memory associated with the macro variable m y i e c be 2 (i.e., two expanded variables). The first macro rule corresponds to two plain rules each of which contains one possible instantiation of x. Similarly, the second macro rule corresponds to four plain rules because of the two possible instantiations for x and two possible instantiations for y, yielding a total of four combinations. div.p: Figure 1 illustrates the execution model of the MRL language. An MRL program can be expanded only when the size of the working memory for each macro variable has been decided. In the first step, the MRL control layer prepares data for the working memory of an MRL program module before rule firing starts. At this point, the size of the working memory is fixed. Then the program module is executed until it reaches a fixed point. The result of the execution is the updated contents of the working memory. It will then be used by the control layer and program modules selected in subsequent cycles. Conceptually, the MRL program module is expanded to an EQL program which is executed by an EQL engine. In practice, a more sophisticated match algorithm willbe used to execute MRL programs, as we shall discuss later. We illustrate this technique in the next two sections. We shall first discuss a fixed point detection algorithm for EQL programs. Then we shall show how this algorithm tran~ers to MRL programs. Usually, this is done by combining the proof of the algorithm for EQL and some basic axioms on the relationship of EQL and MRL.

div.head: Timing Analysis of EQL
div.p: Timing analysis of rule-based systems is a non-trivial task even for EQL programs. To tackle this problem, we rely on a method which groups rules into modules so that each module can be analyzed independently. A major issue involved in this approach is establishing conditions which allow modules to be analyzed "independently". For this purpose, we shall introduce the concepts of superposition and rule Clustering.

div.p: We define superposition to be a predicate on two sets of rules. Let P and Q be two disjoint sets of rules. P superposes Q ( P / / Q ) if and only if the following condition holds:

Superposition has the desirable properties described in the following theorems: The reason for rule clustering is to facilitate modular analysis. The advantages are: (1) We can mix different analysis methods in analyzing one program and choose the most suitable method for each set of rules. (2) We can analyze rule-based programs more efficiently because modular analysis is a strategy of divide-and-conquer. It breaks down the state space of the problem into smaller spaces and analyzes them separately. (3) It makes it easier to pinpoint the most pertinent rules that cause the failure of reaching a fixed point. (4) The result of rule clustering can be used as guidance for scheduling and parallel processing.
Following is an algorithm that groups rules into clusters and groups clusters into "self-reliant sets" based on a graph called access graph.

div.head: Timing Analysis of MRL
div.p: In this section, we present the fixed point detection algorithm for MRL, as an example of the transfer principle.

div.head: The MAM Graph
div.p: For MRL programs, we introduce Macro Access-Modify graphs (MAM graphs) which are the counterpart of the AM graphs in EQL. The definitions of cluster, self-reliant set, braid and disagreeable braid can be directly applied to MAM graphs of MRL programs. Hence, Algorithm 1 can be used for MAM graphs without modifications.

It is obvious that the expanded rules of a macro rule may not belong to the same cluster in the expanded AM graph. In other words, the boundary of clusters and selfreliant sets are not preserved after macro expansions. We have to re-consider the properties of clusters and self-reliant sets in MRL. The following theorems define the relationship between clusters and self-reliant sets of a MAM graph and its expanded AM graph. They relate properties in MAM graphs to properties in the corresponding AM graphs.

Theorem 4 Let m and n be rule vertices in the MAMgraph of an MRL program. Suppose m' and n' are expanded rule vertices of m and n respectively. If m ' and n' are in same cluster, then m and n are in the same cluster.

div.head: Disjunctions in Enabling Conditions
div.p: Since the enabling conditions of MRL rules can be ordinary boolean expressions, the first operation of Rhyme is to transform the enabling condition of each rule to its disjunctive normal form. Now, the enabling condition consists of one or more disjuncts, each disjunct consists of one or more conjuncts, and each conjunct contains only arithmetic operators and predicates.

After transforming each enabling condition to its disjunctive normal form, we assign a binding space array (BSA) to the disjunct. Each element in the BSA is called a cell. Each cell contains a set of slots which correspond to variables in this disjunct. We define a cell to be a salient ceZI if and only if all the slots in this cell have been filled? It is our primary goal to design cells, slots of BSAs, and an update method so that if at least one of these BSAs associated with disjuncts of an enabling condition contains a salient cell, then this rule is enabled.

div.head: Designing the Binding Space Arrays
div.p: We construct the binding space arrays according to the following algorithm: Algorithm 3 Constructing binding space arrays.
We assign a dimension of the BSA to each variable in the disjunct.
If a conjunct is a simple equality comparison between two variables, the two variables share a dimension.
The range of a dimension is the intersection of the ranges of all the variables that share this dimension.
If there are n distinct pattern and primitive variables in this disjunct, then n slots are allocated in each cell of this BSA with each slot corresponding to one pattem or primitive variable.

Certain conjuncts can be used as filters to mask out cells if the conjuncts are always evaluated tofalse at these cells. -0 types of conjuncts serve as filters: (1) selective conjuncts, and (2) conjuncts which are not a simple equality comparison between two variables. Readers can find a thorough study in [9]. MRL builds on our previous work with the EQL language. In particular, the EQL-like semantics of MRL enables us to state a transfer principle which relates analysis algorithms of EQL programs to MRL programs. To demonstrate this principle, we have shown the fixed point detection algorithm for EQL. Since the properties tested by these algorithms are independent of macro expansion (i.e., the size of working memory), they can also be used for MRL program analysis.

div.p: We have implemented a package containing timing analysis algorithms for analyzing both EQL and MRL programs. To solve the practical problem of reducing the match time for detecting enabled rules, we have also proposed a match algorithm called Rhyme. Rhyme has important advantages over match algorithms of other rule-based production systems. In particular, Rhyme lends itself to compile-time analysis of time bounds for the match part of expert system execution. It is also amenable to a number of optimization technique on space versus time tradeoff.

figure.head: Principle for Analyz- ing MRL
figure.figDesc: Since macro rules can be expanded to plain rules, it is possible to analyze expanded rules using any algorithms designed for EQL. So why design new algorithms to analyze MRL programs? The answer is because the expansion of macro rules may result in a huge number of plain rules if the number of wmes is large. Analysis of these expanded rules can be computationally expensive. Fortunately, the execution model of MRL allows us to avoid having to expand macro rules to analyze the MRL program. As we have mentioned earlier, we accomplish this by applying a transfer principle. Suppose we know that if an EQL program satisfies a certain property P, then that program must have bounded response time. Suppose further that the MRL program we want to analyze always expands into equivalent EQL programs which satisfy P. It follows immediately from the execution model of MRL that the MRL program will also have bounded response time.
